title: Anthropic in talks to buy Israel's Decart AI for $6 billion
subtitle: The deal would be Anthropic's largest ever, bringing real-time video generation and chip-efficiency software in-house ahead of its IPO.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Bloomberg reported on August 13 that Anthropic is in advanced talks to acquire Decart AI, a Tel Aviv startup, in a deal valued at roughly $6 billion. If it closes, this would be Anthropic's largest known acquisition — larger than any of the smaller research-team and infrastructure pickups it has done in the past year — and it would land in the window just before the S-1 filing the company has been telegraphing.

Decart makes two things worth the price. The first is real-time generative video: its Lucy 2.5 model, released in July, was the first system to hit real-time streaming visual effects on a live video feed, and Oasis 3 is a world model that generates playable simulated environments. The second is the reason the check is $6 billion rather than $1 billion — chip-optimization software that squeezes more useful work out of the same GPU-hours, which for a lab whose compute bill is the largest single item on its P&L is close to a direct multiplier on gross margin.

Anthropic has spent 2026 buying capacity — Riot Platforms' Rockdale campus, the Broadcom-Google infrastructure deal, the Bitdeer-Norway joint venture — and this is the first acquisition aimed at getting more per chip rather than more chips. Read alongside the video capability, the deal also positions the company to compete directly with OpenAI's Sora line and Google's Veo without spending two years training a video foundation model from scratch. The talks are not finalized and could still fall apart.

Takeaway for learners: acquisitions in AI often look like they are about the model but are actually about the org chart. Anthropic isn't buying Decart for Lucy 2.5 in isolation — the video model will be old inside a year — but for the team that knows how to build the next one and the systems people who know how to make chips run harder. When you evaluate a startup deal, ask which of those two things the acquirer is really writing the check for. It's almost never the current product.
